Interactive series · Six parts

Neural Networks Learn by Being Wrong

No matter how big deep learning gets, if you open it up, it repeats three jobs. A perceptron multiplies and adds numbers to make a decision, a cost function measures how wrong that decision was, and normalization puts the numbers on the same scale so the whole process runs smoothly.

This series carries one problem through all six parts. Can we tell if a mail is spam just from its number of links and exclamation marks? You press buttons, change numbers, and learn by watching the pictures and numbers change together.

Shared data · 660 mailsThe mail data

Every part reuses the same data, the same picture (links × exclamation marks) and the same two sets. The result of one part becomes the question of the next.

1Shared data · 660 mails

You can't see learning with just four mails. This series uses the same 660 mails in all six parts. There are four kinds, paired up to make an easy set and a hard set. The same picture (links × exclamation marks) and the same two sets come back in every part.

KindAnswerMailsAvg. charactersAvg. linksAvg. exclamation marksSet
Work emailNormal3001,1960.60.5Easy
Ad spamSpam1206536.87.1Easy
NewsletterNormal1604,1513.81.5Hard
Phishing spamSpam801,5422.72.2Hard

Easy set = work email vs ad spam (420 mails, baseline 0.714) · Hard set = newsletter vs phishing spam (240 mails, baseline 0.667). For each kind of mail, 3/4 was set aside for training and 1/4 for test ahead of time, recorded in the CSV's split column (stratified). This is made-up data built to show the ideas. Download CSV

Series map — six parts in orderSeries map

Parts 1–4 cover one idea each, Part 5 puts them all together for your own experiments, and Part 6 sorts the models again by how they answer. Click a card to go to that part.

How models workImproving performanceHands-on experiments
Part 1

Perceptron — multiply, add, and fix it when wrong

A part that multiplies, adds and compares with a threshold. It turns the line only on mails it gets wrong.

Try this · Turn the line by hand · Press “Train once” · Compare convergence on the easy/hard sets

Part 2

Activation functions — you need a bend to stack layers

A function that bends the score before sending it to the next layer. Without the bend, stacking layers is pointless.

Try this · See the gradients of nine functions · Solve XOR with two hidden neurons · Train with only the activation changed

Part 3

Cost functions and gradient descent — measure how wrong, then go downhill

Measure how wrong you are with one number, then take one step at a time in the direction that makes it smaller.

Try this · Move the penalty curve · Roll the ball · Draw a cost curve with mails · Mini-batches

Part 4

Normalization — put numbers on the same scale

Line up the reference point and scale of the numbers so learning is fast and stable. Plus regularization.

Try this · The moment you add character count · Before vs after standardization · Layer normalization table · Change λ

Part 5

Lab — train while changing just one dial

Pick or make data, change just one dial, train, and judge the result.

Try this · Make your own distribution · Seven dials · Experiment log · Download CSV

Part 6

Models that draw lines and models that give probabilities — regions, probability, numbers

Compare on one screen the models that draw a line (perceptron, SVM), the model that gives a probability (logistic), and the model that answers with a number (linear regression).

Try this · Train three models at once · Make islands with kernel SVC · Click the entropy map · Coins and bells

Questions that link the parts
  1. Part 1 → Part 2One perceptron couldn't solve XOR or the hard set. What function should we use instead of a step?
  2. Part 2 → Part 3We set the weights that solve XOR by hand. To find them from data, what should we make smaller?
  3. Part 3 → Part 4The hard set's cost got stuck at 0.5. Will adding character count fix it? But those numbers are in the thousands.
  4. Part 4 → Part 5We needed both information and scale. Now it's time to turn the dials one by one and check for yourself.
  5. Part 5 → Part 6They use the same straight line, so why does one model only say “spam” while another says “87%”? And how is regression, which asks for a number, different again?

How to use thisHow to use

Nothing to install. All you need is a browser.

Just press buttons

Change a slider or button and the pictures and numbers change right away. Animations can be played, paused and stepped through.

Underlined words

Click a term with a dotted underline to see an analogy and its meaning. Each part ends with a glossary.

Run in Colab

In each part's “Connect to practice” section, download the code as .ipynb and upload it to Colab to run it as is. The beginner code has no def, for or indentation.

For instructors

The answer key page for educators has answers and grading criteria for the check questions, sample answers for the experiment tasks, and lecture notes.

On your phone

It opens on phones too, but with so many pictures and tables it's more comfortable on a PC or tablet.

How to read the numbers

Next to accuracy there's always a baseline (always answering with the bigger class). Accuracy only means something if it beats that line.

Neural Networks Learn by Being Wrong — by Ahn Sangsun (CEO, M-Robo Inc.)

What's an illustrative model · The 660 mails are made-up data built to show the ideas (seed 0). Training in the browser exercises is real, computed right on this page, and results are not carried over or mixed between chapters. But since it's a teaching implementation, initial values and details differ from standard code (scikit-learn), so the numbers may differ slightly. The four example mails, contour shapes and exercise weights from the original explanation are illustrative examples.
